controls.label: Shape
controls.qualification: A sphere of the published radius, lit by Hunor; the neutral gray is a display convention, not a measured color.
controls.notes: No image or color of HAT-P-2 b is published: the sphere has its measured size, and the gray marks an unresolved surface. The lighting is its own star's, at the measured orbit. The gray takes the color of hat-p-2's light, as its color dataset measures it.

controls.label: Day side
controls.qualification: Measured in eclipse at secondary eclipse: Deming et al. 2023, dayside brightness temperature at 4.5 µm (uniform reanalysis of Spitzer's eclipses, CDS J/AJ/165/104 table 2)
controls.notes: The day side of HAT-P-2 b is 2,052 K at secondary eclipse: its brightness temperature at 4.5 µm (Spitzer IRAC), measured from the light lost when the planet passes behind its star. The false color shows that one number over the day side, on a scale every planet shown this way shares. The night side is not measured and is left blank. The orbit is eccentric, so the temperature holds for the moment of eclipse, not round the orbit. With shadows on, the star's light darkens the night half.

charts.alt: The orbits of Hunor's planets in this map from above, to scale, with HAT-P-2 b highlighted and the direction to Earth down. Each orbit is the one the app draws, from the published period, a/R*, eccentricity and argument of periastron; the star is a marker, not to scale.

HAT-P-2 b crossing its star, as TESS recorded it: 3 sectors (52, 78, 79) of the SPOC pipeline's 2-minute light curves of TIC 39903405, each transit divided by a straight line fitted to the light either side and folded onto the orbit the app draws, then averaged in 17-minute bins. Error bars are each bin's standard error.

physical.credit: Radius from Bonomo et al. 2017 (2017A&A...602A.107B), via the NASA Exoplanet Archive; mass from de Beurs et al. 2023, the mass the NASA Exoplanet Archive's composite table adopts (2023AJ....166..136D), via the NASA Exoplanet Archive; orbit from Ment et al. 2018 (2018AJ....156..213M), via the NASA Exoplanet Archive
